w:r.w:t: Detailed Explanations of Findings C1, C3, and C5
Effect of Early vs Late Inguinal Hernia Repair on Serious Adverse Event Rates in Preterm Infants: A Randomized Clinical Trial

This document explains three document-grounded reporting findings from the supplied article package. It uses only the provided main article and results supplement. It does not assess research misconduct, raw-data validity, clinical appropriateness, or information outside the supplied files.
The abstract states that 320 infants underwent operative repair. The article’s arm-specific repair counts show that only 281 infants underwent repair; 320 is the postwithdrawal cohort.
Figure 1 contains 9 infants per arm labeled only as not undergoing treatment as randomized, but does not explicitly identify them as postrandomization withdrawals excluded from the primary analysis.
The Patient Characteristics section directs enrollment-detail readers to eTables 1–2, although only eTable 1 contains enrollment and refusal information; eTable 2 contains outcome analyses.
Abstract Misstates the Number of Infants Who Underwent Operative Repair
The abstract assigns the operative-repair label to the 320-infant postwithdrawal cohort, although the article documents 281 infants who actually underwent hernia repair.

The abstract states that, among 338 randomized infants, “320 underwent operative repair.” The number 320 does not correspond to the reported operative-repair population. It is the number remaining after 9 infants in each randomized arm were withdrawn:
The Surgery Characteristics section reports that 152 of 163 infants in the early-repair arm and 129 of 157 infants in the late-repair arm underwent hernia repair:
152 early repairs + 129 late repairs = 281 operative repairs

Figure 1 independently confirms the same total. In the early arm, 147 infants underwent repair before neonatal intensive care unit discharge and 5 underwent repair after discharge. In the late arm, 90 underwent repair after reaching 55 weeks’ postmenstrual age and 39 underwent repair before reaching 55 weeks.
The difference is 39 infants. Figure 1 and the Surgery Characteristics text report 11 early-arm and 28 late-arm infants who did not undergo hernia repair:
All infants randomized to a timing strategy.
Withdrawn by parents or guardians after randomization.
The cohort mislabeled in the abstract as having undergone repair.
Infants explicitly reported as not receiving repair.
Infants who actually underwent hernia repair.
Infants with complete primary-outcome data; this is a separate population from the operative-repair population.
Nature and limit of the finding.

C1 identifies an incorrect population label in the abstract. It does not, by itself, show that the primary-outcome calculation or the randomized strategy comparison is invalid. The primary outcome is separately reported for 308 infants with complete data.
“Among the 338 randomized infants (172 in the early repair group and 166 in the late repair group), 320 underwent operative repair ...”
“320 underwent operative repair” assigns an operative-exposure label to the postwithdrawal cohort.
PDF p. 4; journal p. 1038; Results—Patient Characteristics.
“After randomization, 9 infants were withdrawn from each treatment group ... leaving 163 in the early inguinal hernia repair group and 157 in the late inguinal hernia repair group.”
This establishes that 320 equals 163 + 157 after the 18 withdrawals.
PDF pp. 4–5; journal pp. 1038–1039; Surgery Characteristics.
“Among 163 infants in the early inguinal hernia repair group, 152 (93%) underwent hernia repair ...”
“Among the 157 infants in the late inguinal hernia repair group, 129 (82%) underwent hernia repair ...”
These arm-specific values produce the documented repair total of 281.
147 repairs before NICU discharge + 5 repairs after discharge = 152.
90 repairs after 55 weeks + 39 repairs before 55 weeks = 129.
If the intended subject is the operative-repair population:
“Among the 320 infants remaining after withdrawal, 281 underwent operative repair.”
If the intended subject is the postwithdrawal cohort:
“Among the 338 randomized infants, 18 were withdrawn after randomization, leaving 320 infants in the postwithdrawal cohort.”
Figure 1 Omits Explicit Withdrawal and Analysis-Exclusion Branches
Figure 1 includes matching 9-infant categories in both randomized arms but does not explicitly identify them as postrandomization withdrawals excluded from the primary analysis.

Figure 1 shows the following sequence in the early arm: 172 randomized, 163 “Received treatment as randomized,” 9 “Did not undergo treatment as randomized,” 4 lost to follow-up, and 159 included in the primary analysis. The late arm shows 166 randomized, 157 “Received treatment as randomized,” 9 “Did not undergo treatment as randomized,” 8 lost to follow-up, and 149 included in the primary analysis.

The Results text and Table 2 note a identify the two 9-infant categories as infants who were withdrawn after randomization and excluded from analysis. Figure 1 does not use the term “withdrawn,” does not state “excluded from primary analysis,” and does not draw a separate withdrawal/exclusion branch before the primary-analysis boxes.

If a reader follows only the explicitly labeled follow-up exclusions in Figure 1, the apparent calculations are 172 − 4 = 168 and 166 − 8 = 158. These do not produce the displayed analysis populations. The reader must infer an additional, unstated step: the two 9-infant categories were withdrawals excluded from analysis.

“Did not undergo treatment as randomized” describes treatment receipt or adherence. “Withdrawn after randomization and excluded from analysis” describes study and analysis status. These concepts are not interchangeable. A participant may deviate from assigned treatment yet remain in the randomized analysis group. Therefore, the Figure 1 wording does not independently communicate the analysis exclusion documented elsewhere.
Nature and limit of the finding.

C3 is a flow-label and branch omission, not an arithmetic error. The final analysis counts are reconcilable and agree with Table 2. The issue is Minor because the Results text and Table 2 note provide the missing status and because the omission does not, by itself, establish an incorrect outcome calculation.
“172 Randomized”; “163 Received treatment as randomized”; “9 Did not undergo treatment as randomized”; “4 Lost to follow-up”; “159 Included in primary analysis.”
“166 Randomized”; “157 Received treatment as randomized”; “9 Did not undergo treatment as randomized”; “8 Lost to follow-up”; “149 Included in primary analysis.”
The matching 9-infant categories are not explicitly labeled as withdrawals or analysis exclusions.
PDF p. 4; journal p. 1038; Results—Patient Characteristics.
“After randomization, 9 infants were withdrawn from each treatment group (they were withdrawn by the parents or guardians because of treatment preferences or for other reasons) ...”
This identifies the status of the two 9-infant categories that Figure 1 labels only by treatment receipt.
PDF p. 4; journal p. 1038; Statistical Analysis.
“The intention-to-treat analyses were performed in the full data set, and included all randomized infants except those withdrawn from the study ...”
The article states that withdrawal determined exclusion from the analysis data set.
PDF p. 6; journal p. 1040; Table 2 note a.
“Excludes 9 infants (in each group) who were withdrawn after randomization and 12 who were lost to follow-up (4 in the early repair group and 8 in the late repair group).”
The note explicitly distinguishes postrandomization withdrawal from loss to follow-up and supplies the complete reconciliation.
Add a separate branch in each randomized arm labeled:
“Withdrawn after randomization and excluded from primary analysis (n = 9)”
“Remaining after withdrawal (n = 163)” in the early arm, followed by 4 lost to follow-up and 159 included in the primary analysis.
“Remaining after withdrawal (n = 157)” in the late arm, followed by 8 lost to follow-up and 149 included in the primary analysis.
Enrollment-Details Cross-Reference Incorrectly Includes Outcome-Analysis eTable 2

The Patient Characteristics section directs readers seeking additional enrollment details to “eTables 1–2,” but only eTable 1 contains the relevant enrollment, eligibility, consent, and refusal information.

The Patient Characteristics section discusses 613 parents or guardians who refused participation. It reports that 280 preferred early repair, 196 preferred late repair, 71 wanted the clinician to decide, and 66 had other reasons. It then states that “additional enrollment details appear in eTables 1-2.”

eTable 1 directly supports and expands this paragraph. Its title is “Additional information related to trial enrollment,” and it lists eligibility-related factors, reasons for refusal by parents or guardians, reasons for refusal by physicians, and other reasons eligible infants were not consented.

eTable 2 has a different purpose. Its title is “Frequentist primary and major secondary outcome analyses.” It reports serious-adverse-event results, hospital-day results, effect estimates, confidence intervals, P values, and statistical models. It does not provide the refusal breakdown referenced by the Patient Characteristics paragraph.
Other reasons eligible infants were not consented
Frequentist confidence intervals and P values

Figure 1 note b correctly directs additional enrollment information to eTable 1 alone. The Primary Outcome section correctly directs frequentist outcome-analysis readers to eTable 2. These two content-appropriate citations reinforce that the Patient Characteristics reference should identify eTable 1 rather than the range eTables 1–2.
Nature and limit of the finding.

C5 is a cross-reference error, not a numerical or statistical-result error. The correct destination, eTable 1, is already included in the printed range, so readers can still locate the enrollment information. eTable 2 itself is not erroneous and is correctly cited elsewhere. These factors support Minor severity.
PDF p. 4; journal p. 1038; Results—Patient Characteristics.

“Of these 613 parents or guardians, 280 preferred early repair, 196 preferred late repair, 71 wanted the clinician to decide, and 66 had other reasons (additional enrollment details appear in eTables 1-2 and details of the randomization by study site appear in eTable 3 in Supplement 3).”
“eTable 1. Additional information related to trial enrollment”
eligibility-related factors; reasons for refusal by parents/guardians (n = 613); reasons for refusal by physicians (n = 37); and other reasons eligible infants were not consented (n = 16).
“eTable 2. Frequentist primary and major secondary outcome analyses”
44/159 versus 27/149 serious-adverse-event counts; risk difference −9.0%; relative risk 0.65; confidence intervals; P values; hospital-day results; and statistical-model descriptions.
These contents do not supply the enrollment-refusal information discussed in the cited main-text paragraph.

Qualification regarding the text below eTable 2

A short paragraph below eTable 2 describes participating centers and notes that site-level randomization counts are provided below. It does not provide the enrollment-refusal breakdown discussed in the Patient Characteristics paragraph. The main article separately assigns randomization-by-site details to eTable 3. This paragraph therefore does not resolve the cross-reference mismatch.
“Additional enrollment details appear in eTable 1, and details of randomization by study site appear in eTable 3 in Supplement 3.”
